extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (agents/attorneys) involved in prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying, framing, and making statutory and nonstatutory (obviousness-type and other) double patenting rejections during patent examination, including proper form-paragraph usage and when terminal disclaimers or additional statutory rejections are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory (same invention) double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 as claiming the same invention as that of claim [2] of prior U.S. Patent No. [3]. This is a double patenting rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 8.31 (must be preceded by form paragraph 8.30/form paragraph 1). Used only where the "scope" of the inventions claimed is identical. Do not use this paragraph if conflicting claims are in another copending application (use provisional double patenting form paragraph 8.32 instead). In bracket 3 insert the number of the conflicting patent. If the patent is to a different inventive entity and is commonly assigned, also use form paragraph 8.27 to require the assignee to name the first inventor. If evidence indicates the patent is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) or (g), also make rejections using form paragraphs 7.15 and/or 7.19; if the patent has an earlier effective U.S. filing date, also consider a 102(e) rejection using form paragraph 7.15.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional rejection for statutory double patenting (copending application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] provisionally rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 as claiming the same invention as that of claim [2] of copending Application No. [3]. This is a provisional double patenting rejection since the conflicting claims have not in fact been patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 8.32 and precede it with form paragraph 8.30. Use only for conflicting claims in another copending application (not an issued patent). In bracket 3 insert the number of the conflicting application. Do not use for nonstatutory-type double patenting (use 8.33–8.39). If the copending application is by a different inventive entity and commonly assigned, use form paragraph 8.27 as well. If evidence shows prior-art relationships under 102(f)/(g), make additional rejections (7.15/7.19). If applications do not have the same inventive entity and effective filing date, consider making a provisional 102(e) rejection in the later-filed application (form paragraph 7.15.01).

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer cannot overcome statutory double patenting rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: The filing of a terminal disclaimer cannot overcome a double patenting rejection based upon 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminal disclaimers may not be used to overcome a statutory (same-invention) double patenting rejection. (Terminal disclaimers are discussed elsewhere for nonstatutory double patenting relief.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstatutory double patenting (obviousness-type)
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonstatutory obviousness-type double patenting rejection is appropriate where the conflicting claims are not identical, but at least one examined application claim is not patentably distinct from the reference claim(s) because the examined application claim is either anticipated by, or would have been obvious over, the reference claim(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on a judicially created doctrine grounded in public policy to prevent unjustified timewise extension of the right to exclude. It is "analogous to [a failure to meet] the nonobviousness requirement of 35 U.S.C. 103" except that the patent principally underlying the double patenting rejection is not considered prior art. Use form paragraph 8.33 as a heading (once) before any of form paragraphs 8.34–8.39. A timely filed terminal disclaimer in compliance with 37 CFR 1.321(c) or (d) may be used to overcome an actual or provisional rejection based on a nonstatutory double patenting ground provided the conflicting application or patent either is shown to be commonly owned with this application, or claims an invention made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of a joint research agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries for obviousness-type double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining obviousness-type double patenting, apply the Graham v. John Deere factual inquiries used for 35 U.S.C. 103 obviousness determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The factual inquiries are summarized as: (A) Determine the scope and content of a patent claim relative to a claim in the application at issue; (B) Determine the differences between the scope and content of the patent claim and the claim in the application; (C) Determine the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; and (D) Evaluate any objective indicia of nonobviousness. The conclusion is made in light of these determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness-type rejection must state differences and reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Any obviousness-type double patenting rejection should make clear: (A) The differences between the inventions defined by the conflicting claims — a claim in the patent compared to a claim in the application; and (B) The reasons why a person of ordinary skill in the art would conclude that the invention defined in the claim at issue is anticipated by, or would have been an obvious variation of, the invention defined in a claim in the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit rationale in the action (e.g., in bracket [4] or [5] of the form paragraphs) explaining why claims are not patentably distinct; if using secondary references, explain the obviousness rationale. Do not treat the patent disclosure as prior art when making the obviousness determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of patent disclosure/specification in obviousness-type analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosure of the patent may not be used as prior art, but the specification can be used as a dictionary to learn the meaning of a term and those portions which provide support for the patent claims may be examined when addressing whether an application claim defines an obvious variation of an invention claimed in the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite cases: Toro Co. v. White Consol. Indus., Renishaw PLC v. Marposs. Use disclosure to determine proper meanings of claim terms and to identify portions of the specification that support the patent claims; do not use the patent as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-way obviousness test (when appropriate)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the application at issue is the later filed application or both are filed on the same day, only a one-way determination of obviousness is needed in resolving the issue of double patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the invention defined in a claim in the application would have been anticipated by, or an obvious variation of, the invention defined in a claim in the patent. Unless a claimed invention in the application would have been anticipated or obvious over a claimed invention in the patent, no obviousness-type double patenting rejection should be made. One-way test is appropriate absent administrative delay or inability to have filed claims in a single application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way obviousness test (when required)
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-way test is to be applied only when the applicant could not have filed the claims in a single application and there is administrative delay; when the patent is the later filed application, the question whether timewise extension is justified must be addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the Graham analysis twice — once with application claims as the claims in issue and once with the patent claims as the claims in issue. An obvious-type double patenting rejection is appropriate only where each analysis compels a conclusion that the invention defined in the claims in issue is an obvious variation of the invention defined in a claim in the other application/patent. Burden may shift to applicant to show why a two-way determination is required. Consider factors indicating administrative delay (appeals, interferences, Office delay) versus applicant-caused delay (requests for extensions, strategic continuations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form-paragraph selection and sequencing for obviousness-type rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph 8.33 is a 'Heading' only and must precede any one of form paragraphs 8.34 to 8.39; use specific form paragraphs depending on whether the primary reference is an issued patent or a copending application and whether secondary references are involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 8.34: Rejection, Obviousness Type Double Patenting - No Secondary Reference(s) (use when primary reference is a patent). 8.35: Provisional Rejection, Obviousness Type - No Secondary Reference(s) (use for copending application primary). 8.36: Rejection, Obviousness Type - With Secondary Reference(s) (primary reference is patent, insert secondary reference in bracket 4). 8.37: Provisional Rejection, Obviousness Type - With Secondary Reference(s) (primary reference is application). Always ensure 8.33 precedes the chosen paragraph and is used only once in an Office action. Insert appropriate bracketed information (claim numbers, patent/app numbers, secondary refs, and explanatory rationale).

rubrics_metrics.name: Schneller-type (other) nonstatutory double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: There are unique circumstances (illustrated by In re Schneller) where another type of nonstatutory double patenting rejection is applicable even where the inventions claimed are nonobvious over each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schneller situations are fact-specific and will be rare. The Technology Center (TC) Director must approve any nonstatutory double patenting rejections based on Schneller. Examiner should consult SPE and obtain TC Director approval before making such a rejection. Use form paragraphs 8.33 and the appropriate one of form paragraphs 8.38 (between an issued patent and one or more applications) and 8.39 (provisional rejections) for this type.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to make additional 102/103 rejections along with double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: If evidence is of record to indicate that the patent is prior art under either 35 U.S.C. 102(f) or (g), a rejection should also be made using form paragraphs 7.15 and/or 7.19 in addition to this double patenting rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent is to a different inventive entity and the effective U.S. filing date of the patent antedates the effective filing date of the application, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) should additionally be made using form paragraph 7.15.02. For obviousness-type double patenting with secondary references, if the conflicting patent is prior art under 102(f)/(g), make an additional 102/103 rejection using form paragraph 7.21 unless disqualified under 103(c). For copending applications with differing inventive entities and filing dates, consider form paragraph 7.21.01 to make a 102(e)/103(a) rejection in the later-filed application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural ownership and joint research agreement conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraphs may be used only where the conflicting invention is: (a) by the same inventive entity; (b) by a different inventive entity and is commonly assigned even though there is no common inventor; (c) not commonly assigned but has at least one common inventor; or (d) made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of a joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using form paragraphs (statutory or nonstatutory), ensure the ownership/status facts fit one of these categories. If the conflicting application/patent is currently commonly assigned but the file does not establish that the inventions were commonly owned at the time the later invention was made, use form paragraph 8.28 in addition to resolve priority issues under 102(f) and/or (g). Terminal disclaimer relief for nonstatutory rejections requires showing common ownership or JRA. Insert appropriate bracketed ownership information as needed.
